To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

successful regulation of affect is partly dependent on the ability to modulate negative emotion through the use of top-down cognitive control mechanisms, and that successful emotion regulation is associated with increased functional connectivity within the limbic-frontal brain system.

(a) successful emotion regulation involves the modulation of negative emotional responses through cognitive strategies (e.g., reappraisal); (b) this modulation is associated with the recruitment of specific areas of the prefrontal cortex (dorsomedial, orbital, anterior cingulated); (c) these areas are functionally interconnected with the amygdala during emotion regulation, and the strength of this coupling predicts the extent to which negative emotional responses are attenuated.

Successful control of affect depends on the capacity of the brain to modulate negative responses through cognitive strategies, and that this capacity partly depends on the functional connectivity between the limbic system and prefrontal cortical regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying the ability to modulate negative emotions.
understanding the neural basis of emotion regulation.
the neural basis of emotion regulation and its role in psychopathology, particularly anxiety disorders and depression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
amygdala-frontal functional connectivity during emotion regulation is a critical determinant of the success of emotion regulation.
the amygdala and frontal cortex are functionally connected and this connectivity is important for emotion regulation

the strength of functional connectivity between the amygdala and frontal cortex predicts the effectiveness of cognitive reappraisal of emotional stimuli, with greater connectivity associated with greater emotion regulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability to regulate emotion involves the capacity to engage frontal regions in a way that modulates the activity of the amygdala.
the ability to regulate emotion depends on the functional connectivity of the amygdala with prefrontal cortical regions.
successful regulation of affect depends on a functional coupling between the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex, and that this coupling is modulated by the use of specific cognitive strategies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
emotion regulation is a dynamic process that requires the coordination of activity between brain areas that are involved in the generation and modulation of emotion.
the success of emotion regulation is dependent not only on the ability to activate frontal regions, but also on the ability of these regions to communicate effectively with the amygdala.
successful emotion regulation depends, to some extent, on the strength of connectivity between the amygdala and frontal regions.
